trajectory.position_description: He continues to treat the Crofts as acceptable but inferior, with no real warmth or egalitarian shift.

Continued social acceptance of the Crofts

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Sir Walter moves from naval disdain to practical acceptance. The change is limited, but it is real: status management replaces outright contempt.

relational_axes.axis_name: From qualified deference to condescending dismissal
relational_axes.pole_start: He begins with practical deference to Lady Russell as a household adviser, though his esteem is always limited by vanity and sensitivity to criticism.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends more openly dismissive, using her judgment only when convenient and otherwise treating her as inferior in taste and social discernment.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Lady Russell remains an authority figure Sir Walter cannot fully ignore, but his emotional stance shifts from reluctant consultation to sharper contempt whenever her judgment challenges his vanity.

relational_axes.axis_name: From useful flattery to embarrassed distrust
relational_axes.pole_start: He treats Mrs Clay as a pleasant, useful, and flattering presence in the household, with some attraction and little self-awareness about the risks she poses.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends shocked and mortified by her disappearance and deception, though the reaction is mainly social embarrassment rather than moral insight.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Sir Walter never develops genuine trust or intimacy with Mrs Clay. The change is from pleased usefulness to embarrassed distrust, driven by the collapse of a flattering arrangement.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: This relational axis is well grounded in Austen scholarship: Mrs Clay is repeatedly read as a socially mobile, flattering presence whose proximity to Sir Walter exposes his vanity and class blindness, while the eventual revelation of her attachment to William Elliot produces chiefly embarrassment and social damage rather than moral self-correction. Structural and gender-focused readings of Persuasion commonly treat the Sir Walter–Mrs Clay dynamic as a small but telling plot of misplaced trust, flirtation, and social risk.
